messages.content: Lesson 101: Serialization patterns

Save state to disk or network. Binary: compact, fast, fragile (version changes break it). Text: verbose, slow, human-readable, robust.
Urho3D: XML for scenes/materials/UI (pugixml). JSON for data files. Binary for network messages (VectorBuffer).
Attributes: URHO3D_ACCESSOR_ATTRIBUTE auto-serializes component state. Register in RegisterObject().
Lesson 102: XML in Urho3D

XMLFile: cache->GetResource<XMLFile>(path). GetRoot() returns XMLElement.
Read: element.GetAttribute("name"), GetChild("child"), GetFloat("value").
Write: element.SetAttribute("name", "value"), CreateChild("child").
Scene XML: <scene><node><component type="StaticModel"><attribute name="Model" value="..."/></component></node></scene>.
All Urho3D scene save/load uses this format.
Lesson 103: JSON in Urho3D

JSONFile: cache->GetResource<JSONFile>(path). GetRoot() returns JSONValue.
Read: root["key"].GetString(), root["array"][i].GetFloat().
Used for: DrivenKeys curves, habitat rules, theme preferences, training data.
Prefer JSON over XML for new data files — cleaner syntax, easier to parse by hand.
Lesson 104: Binary serialization

VectorBuffer: write side. buf.WriteU16(count), WriteFloat(x), WriteString(s).
MemoryBuffer: read side. msg.ReadU16(), ReadFloat(), ReadString().
Order matters — read in same order as written. No self-describing format.
Used for: all network protocol messages. Compact, fast, zero overhead.
Lesson 105: Pathfinding

A*: find shortest path on a graph. Open set (candidates), closed set (visited).
Cost: g(n) = actual cost from start. h(n) = heuristic estimate to goal. f(n) = g + h.
Expand lowest f(n) first. Heuristic must never overestimate (admissible).
Urho3D: NavigationMesh + CrowdManager. Recast builds navmesh, Detour does pathfinding.
Lesson 106: Navigation meshes

Walkable surface simplified to connected polygons. Agents walk on the mesh surface.
Recast: builds navmesh from scene geometry. Voxelizes, filters, polygonizes.
Detour: runtime pathfinding on the navmesh. FindPath returns a corridor of polygons.
DetourCrowd: multiple agents avoiding each other. SetMaxSpeed, SetMaxAccel.
Urho3D: NavigationMesh::Build(), CrowdAgent component on NPC nodes.
Lesson 107: Flocking behavior

Three rules: separation (avoid crowding), alignment (match heading), cohesion (steer toward center).
Each agent looks at nearby neighbors. Weighted sum of three forces.
Spatial hash makes neighbor queries fast — don't check all agents.
SchoolFish uses this: SchoolState caches centroid + averageHeading per frame. Members read shared cache.
Lesson 108: Behavior priorities

NPC tasks are priority ordered. FLEE > DEFEND > EAT > HUNT > ... > IDLE.
Higher priority interrupts lower. Task system re-evaluates each tick.
Pick highest-priority task whose conditions are met. Skip tasks with missing prereqs.
Simpler than behavior trees — one flat priority list with condition checks. Easier to debug.
Lesson 109: Finite state machines for AI

States: IDLE, PATROL, CHASE, ATTACK, FLEE. Transitions: conditions that switch states.
Each state: OnEnter (setup), OnUpdate (per-tick behavior), OnExit (cleanup).
Only one state active. Transitions are edges in a graph.
Simple AI: switch(state) in update. Complex AI: state objects with virtual Enter/Update/Exit.
Lesson 110: Decision making

d20 system: roll + skill vs difficulty class (DC). Success if roll+skill >= DC.
Weighted random: probability tables for loot, spawn selection, behavior variety.
Utility AI: score each possible action, pick highest. More nuanced than priority lists.
This game uses d20 for crafting, combat, fishing, trapping. DC scales with item tier.
Lesson 111: Post-processing effects

Full-screen passes after the main render. Read framebuffer, write modified version.
Common: bloom (bright areas glow), blur, SSAO (ambient occlusion), tone mapping.
God rays: radial blur from sun/moon position. WaterDroplets: procedural rain on camera.
Urho3D: render path commands with 'quad' type. Shader reads scene texture, outputs modified.
Lesson 112: Render targets

Render to texture instead of screen. Then use that texture in another pass.
G-Buffer: multiple render targets (MRT) — position, normal, albedo, specular in one pass.
Shadow maps: render scene from light's perspective to depth texture.
Urho3D: RenderSurface on Texture2D. Viewport can target any surface.
Lesson 113: Depth buffer

Per-pixel depth value. Closer pixels overwrite farther ones — correct occlusion.
Depth test: compare new fragment's depth against stored depth. CMP_LESSEQUAL = closer wins.
Depth write: store new depth after passing test. Disable for transparent objects.
Depth buffer precision: more bits near camera, less far away. Keep near plane as far as possible.
Lesson 114: Alpha blending

Transparent rendering. Final = src * srcAlpha + dst * (1 - srcAlpha).
Requires back-to-front sort — further objects rendered first so closer ones blend on top.
Can't use depth test normally — disable depth write, keep depth read.
Opaques first (any order), then transparents sorted back-to-front.
Lesson 115: Normal mapping

Fake surface detail without extra geometry. Normal map stores per-pixel surface direction.
RGB = XYZ of the normal in tangent space. Blue-dominant = mostly flat, varies = bumpy.
Fragment shader reads normal map instead of using interpolated vertex normal.
Result: flat surface looks like it has bricks, pores, scratches. Zero extra triangles.
Lesson 116: Instancing

Draw many copies of the same mesh in one draw call. Each instance has its own transform.
GPU reads per-instance data from a buffer — position, rotation, scale, color.
Massive speedup for: grass, trees, particles, crowds.
Urho3D: auto-batches StaticModels that share Model+Material. No code needed.
Manual: VulkanInstanceBufferManager for explicit instanced draws.
Lesson 117: Terrain rendering

Heightmap: grayscale image where brightness = elevation. 1025x1025 for this game.
Patches: terrain divided into sub-meshes for culling and LOD. 32x32 patches.
Texture splatting: blend multiple textures (grass, rock, sand) using a weight map.
TerrainBlend.glsl: reads weight map, mixes 4 material layers per pixel.
Spacing: world units per heightmap pixel. (2, 0.5, 2) = 2m horizontal, 0.5m vertical per pixel.
Lesson 118: Water rendering

Flat plane at Y=5.0 with shader magic.
Refraction: render scene below water, distort by normal map.
Reflection: render scene mirrored, sample from above.
Fresnel: blend reflection/refraction based on view angle — steep = more refraction, shallow = more reflection.
Depth coloring: deeper = darker/more blue. Water.glsl reads depth buffer.
Lesson 119: Shadow mapping

Render scene from light's POV into depth texture (shadow map).
When rendering main view: project each pixel into shadow map space. If depth > stored depth, pixel is in shadow.
Artifacts: shadow acne (bias fixes), peter panning (too much bias), aliasing (larger shadow map or CSM).
CSM: cascaded shadow maps — multiple shadow maps at different scales for different distances.
Lesson 120: Vulkan vs OpenGL

OpenGL: high-level, driver manages state. Easy to use, less control.
Vulkan: low-level, you manage everything — memory, sync, command buffers, pipelines.
Vulkan advantages: less CPU overhead, explicit multi-threading, predictable performance.
Vulkan disadvantages: 10x more code for same result, easy to deadlock or corrupt memory.
This engine supports both: *_OGL() and *_Vulkan() dispatch pattern.
Lesson 121: Vulkan synchronization

Fences: CPU waits for GPU to finish. Used per-frame to avoid overwriting in-flight resources.
Semaphores: GPU-GPU sync. Image acquired → render → present.
Pipeline barriers: memory/execution ordering within command buffers.
Triple buffering: 3 frame resource sets. While GPU renders frame N, CPU prepares N+1.
Get this wrong = flickering, corruption, or deadlock. The hardest part of Vulkan.
Lesson 122: Vulkan descriptor sets

How shaders access resources (textures, uniform buffers, samplers).
Descriptor set layout: declares what bindings a shader expects.
Descriptor pool: allocates sets from pre-sized pool.
Bind: vkCmdBindDescriptorSets before draw calls.
This engine's known limitation: texture descriptors not fully bound yet — why grass doesn't render.
Lesson 123: Vulkan pipelines

Complete GPU state: shaders, vertex format, blend mode, depth test, cull mode, topology.
Immutable once created — state changes require different pipeline. Cache by hash.
Expensive to create (shader compilation) — do at load time, not per-frame.
This engine: VulkanPipelineCache persists compiled pipelines to disk. Delete cache after shader edits.
Lesson 124: Memory management in Vulkan

GPU memory: you allocate, you track, you free. No garbage collector.
VMA (Vulkan Memory Allocator): library that handles sub-allocation. This engine uses it.
Device local: fast GPU memory. Host visible: CPU can write. Staging: host visible buffer used to upload to device local.
Never leak GPU memory — unlike CPU leaks, GPU memory is scarce and not recoverable.
Lesson 125: Command buffers

Record GPU commands into a buffer, then submit the whole buffer at once.
Begin → bind pipeline → bind descriptors → bind vertex/index → draw → end.
Per-frame: one primary command buffer. Can use secondary buffers for parallel recording.
This engine: per-frame command buffers with triple buffering. Reset at frame start.
Lesson 126: Error handling strategies

Return codes: bool success = DoThing(). Caller checks. Simple, no overhead.
Exceptions: throw on failure, catch at boundary. C++ exceptions are expensive on failure path.
Assertions: debug-only crashes for impossible conditions.
Rule: validate at system boundaries (user input, network, file I/O). Trust internal code.
This codebase: return bool for fallible operations, URHO3D_LOGERROR for diagnostics, no exceptions.
Lesson 127: Design patterns — Singleton

One instance globally accessible. GetSubsystem<T>() in Urho3D.
Good for: engine subsystems (Graphics, Audio, ResourceCache, Network).
Bad when overused — everything becomes global state. Hard to test, hard to reason about.
Urho3D Context holds all subsystems. RegisterSubsystem/GetSubsystem manage the map.
Lesson 128: Design patterns — Observer

Publisher sends events, subscribers receive them. Decoupled communication.
Urho3D event system IS the observer pattern. SubscribeToEvent/SendEvent.
Strengths: sender doesn't know receivers. Add new handlers without modifying sender.
Weakness: hard to trace event flow. Debug by searching for event name across codebase.
Lesson 129: Design patterns — Factory

Create objects by name/type without knowing the concrete class.
Urho3D: context->CreateObject(typeName) uses registered factories.
RegisterFactory<MyComponent>() in Start(). Engine can instantiate from XML/network.
All Component subclasses must register: URHO3D_OBJECT macro + RegisterObject().
Lesson 130: Design patterns — Command

Encapsulate an action as an object. Can be queued, undone, replayed.
Network messages are commands: MSG_ATTACK = 'attack this target'. Server executes.
Build queue in WorkboardManager: EnqueueBuild(target, requester). Processed sequentially.
Undo: store inverse command. This codebase doesn't have undo, but the pattern enables it.
Lesson 131: Bit manipulation

Flags: unsigned flags = FLAG_A | FLAG_B. Test: if (flags & FLAG_A). Clear: flags &= ~FLAG_A.
Power of 2: (x & (x-1)) == 0. Next power of 2: bit tricks.
Byte packing: store 4 values in one int. (a << 24) | (b << 16) | (c << 8) | d.
Used in: hash computation, GPU state packing, protocol message flags.
Lesson 132: Endianness

Byte order in multi-byte values. Little-endian: LSB first (x86). Big-endian: MSB first (network).
Network byte order is big-endian. htonl/ntohl convert.
Urho3D handles this in network serialization — VectorBuffer writes in consistent order.
Only matters when: reading binary files from other platforms, raw network protocols.
Lesson 133: Floating point precision

float: 32-bit, ~7 decimal digits. double: 64-bit, ~15 digits.
float is enough for positions within ~10km. Beyond that: jitter (far from origin).
Never compare floats with ==. Use: Abs(a - b) < epsilon.
Special values: NaN (0/0), Inf (1/0), -Inf (-1/0). IsNaN() checks for corruption.
This engine uses float everywhere. Game world is <2km — well within precision.
Lesson 134: Color representation

RGBA: Red, Green, Blue, Alpha. Each 0.0-1.0 (float) or 0-255 (byte).
Urho3D: Color(r, g, b, a). Color::WHITE, Color::BLACK, Color::RED.
HSV: Hue (angle), Saturation (0-1), Value (0-1). Better for color picking/shifting.
Linear vs sRGB: GPU works in linear, display is sRGB. Gamma correction at output.
Lesson 135: Vertex formats

Each vertex has attributes: position (vec3), normal (vec3), UV (vec2), color (vec4), tangent (vec4).
Vertex buffer: packed array of vertices. Stride = sizeof one vertex.
Index buffer: triangle indices into vertex buffer. 3 indices per triangle.
Urho3D: VertexBuffer, IndexBuffer. Model contains both. Geometry references them.
Lesson 136: Draw calls

Each draw call = one GPU submission. Expensive overhead per call.
Batching: combine objects with same material into one draw. Fewer calls = faster.
Instancing: one draw call for many copies of same mesh.
Target: <1000 draw calls per frame for smooth performance. ProfilerUI shows the count.
Urho3D auto-batches where possible. Use shared materials to help.
Lesson 137: Texture atlasing

Multiple small textures packed into one large texture. Reduces material switches.
UV coordinates adjusted to reference the sub-region. (u*scale+offset, v*scale+offset).
Font atlases: all glyphs in one texture. UI rendering: one draw call for all text.
Trade-off: less flexibility (can't tile individual textures), atlas management complexity.
Lesson 138: Scene streaming

Don't load the entire world at once. Load chunks around the player.
Load zone: async load when player approaches. Unload zone: when player is far.
Urho3D: Scene::LoadAsyncXML for background loading. Connection::SetScene for network.
Future in this game: multi-terrain expansion. Load adjacent terrains on demand.
Lesson 139: Time of day

Sun position from time: elevation = sin(time * 2π / dayLength), azimuth rotates.
Light color shifts: warm orange at dawn/dusk, white at noon, blue at twilight.
Moon independent: own phase cycle, own light contribution.
This game: Melbourne clock display, time scrub slider, classical piano at night.
Consumables tick on real wallclock — immune to time scrub.
Lesson 140: Weather systems

Cloud coverage → rainfall probability → rain particle + audio.
Rainfall accumulates: 256x256 texture, cloud-driven deposit, soil moisture decay.
Wind affects: grass, trees, particle direction, cloud movement.
Audio layers: RainLight/RainHeavy crossfade, wind intensity, muffled sounds under clouds.
Weather drives ecosystem: moisture → vegetation growth → animal food → population.
Lesson 141: Terrain generation

Perlin noise: base terrain shape. Multiple octaves for detail.
Ridged multifractal: mountain ridges (1 - |noise|) creates sharp peaks.
Terracing: quantize heights into plateau levels.
Hydraulic erosion: simulate water flow, carve valleys, deposit sediment.
Island mask: radial falloff to create water-bordered islands.
All in TerrainGenerator. Seed-based: same seed = same terrain.
Lesson 142: Procedural content

Generate content from rules instead of hand-crafting. Infinite variety from finite rules.
Terrain: Perlin noise + erosion. Trees: L-systems. Names: syllable combination.
Advantages: variety, small storage, no artist bottleneck.
Disadvantages: less control, quality variance, hard to make 'specific' things.
Balance: procedural base + hand-placed points of interest.
Lesson 143: Save systems

What to save: player state, world changes, NPC state, time.
Where: SQLite databases (WorldDB). Atomic writes with transactions.
When: periodic checkpoints (every 5 min), on disconnect, on shutdown.
Migration: schema changes between versions. Add columns with defaults, never remove.
This game: dual DB — rules (static, read-only) + world (dynamic, WAL mode).
Lesson 144: Database transactions

BEGIN TRANSACTION → multiple INSERT/UPDATE → COMMIT. All-or-nothing.
If crash between BEGIN and COMMIT: changes are rolled back. Data stays consistent.
WAL mode: readers don't block writers. Better concurrency than default journal.
Always wrap multi-row writes in transactions. Single INSERT is auto-transactional.
Lesson 145: Input handling

Poll: check state each frame. IsKeyDown(KEY_W) — is W currently pressed?
Event: react to changes. E_KEYDOWN fires once on press. E_KEYUP on release.
Mouse: GetMousePosition(), IsMouseButtonDown(). Mouse modes: FREE, RELATIVE, WRAP.
Urho3D: GetSubsystem<Input>(). Mouse mode set in sample's InitMouseMode().
Lesson 146: Camera controls

FPS: mouse rotates, WASD moves. Camera on a node, apply rotation + translation per frame.
Orbit: rotate around a target point. Distance + pitch + yaw.
God cam: top-down, scroll to zoom, edge-pan or WASD. Primary mode in this game.
Possession: camera follows possessed NPC. Third-person offset.
Smooth: lerp position/rotation toward target each frame. Avoid instant snaps.
Lesson 147: Inventory systems

Slots: fixed array of items. Each slot: item_id, quantity, durability.
Weight: each item has weight. Total weight affects movement speed.
Equip slots: hand, offhand, head, body, feet. Separate from bag.
Craft: check recipe inputs against inventory, consume inputs, add output.
This game: WorldDB stores inventory. Server authoritative. Client shows UI.
Lesson 148: Crafting systems

Recipe: input items + quantities → output item. Optional: tool requirement, station requirement, skill gate.
DC check: d20 + skill >= DC. Fail = lose some inputs (crafting failure).
Tier progression: stone (DC 8) → copper → bronze → iron (DC 20) → steel (DC 23).
Station: must be near the right building (Kiln, Forge, Loom). Checked by station_req.
Lesson 149: Building systems

Placement: ghost model preview at cursor. Snap to grid or free placement.
Build: consume materials from inventory. NPC walks to site, plays build animation.
HP: buildings take damage from predators, weather. Repair via STASK_REPAIR.
Types: shelter, storage, crafting station, defense, community.
Ghost models: translucent preview showing footprint before committing.
Lesson 150: Skill systems

XP from doing: each task awards XP to its associated skill.
Skill level = f(total XP). Diminishing returns — higher levels take more XP.
Gates: recipe tier requires minimum skill. DC increases with tier.
Specialization: master (skill 8+) grants settlement-wide buffs.
Teaching: STASK_TEACH transfers 2x XP from teacher to apprentice near campfire.
Lesson 151: Population dynamics

NPCs breed: mate pairs with breed cooldown. Child spawns near mother.
Mortality: starvation, dehydration, hypothermia, combat, drowning.
Growth pressure: food surplus → more breeding. Famine → starvation deaths.
Expansion: settlement at capacity → found new settlement on unclaimed patch.
This creates natural population waves — boom during good seasons, crash in winter.
Lesson 152: Trade systems

NPC-to-NPC: surplus/need swap. Both must have Trade skill 1+.
Mechanism: compare inventories, swap items where one has surplus and other has need.
Player trade: T-key, split window UI (6+6 slots), lock→confirm flow.
Server validates: proximity (5m), combat interrupt, cooldown (5s).
Innovation: EFFICIENT_TRADE allows trading 2 items per exchange.
Lesson 153: Combat systems

d20 + attack vs defense. Weapon: min/max damage, range, slot.
Armor: defense per slot (body, offhand). Stacks.
Situational modifiers: terrain, time of day, status effects.
Death: HP → 0. Server broadcasts MSG_CREATURE_DEATH with cause.
Wolf packs: cooperative flanking reduces defender's defense.
Lesson 154: Death and respawn

Server-tracked death causes: starvation, dehydration, hypothermia, combat, drowning.
Death event: broadcast to clients, play death animation, remove after timer.
Grave marker: STASK_BURY places marker, transfers knowledge from elder.
Respawn: NPCs don't respawn individually — population managed at settlement level.
Player death: death screen, respawn at campfire.
Lesson 155: Fire as gameplay

Core survival loop: fire protects from cold and predators at night.
Fuel management: real-time consumption. Run out → EMBERS → wolves come.
Friction ignition: 2-hour process. Needs skill, materials, uninterrupted time.
Torch carrying: light from fire, carry to dark areas or allied camps.
Signal fires: chieftain lights watchtower fire to alert settlement.
Lesson 156: Ecosystem simulation

Vegetation: 1024x1024 map. Grass/shrub/tree density per pixel.
Moisture: rainfall → soil → plants. Drought kills vegetation.
Animals: habitat rules place species by biome. Grazing reduces local vegetation.
Food chain: herbivores eat plants, predators eat herbivores. Population follows food.
Balance: overhunting → prey collapse → predator starvation → prey recovery.
Lesson 157: Mining and metallurgy

Metal deposits: RGBA texture. R=quantity, G=type, B=purity, A=depth.
Mining: STASK_MINE at exposed deposit. Skill check, ore to inventory, deposit depletes.
Smelting: ore + fuel at station → ingot. Higher tier needs better station.
Trace elements: depth-gated rare ores. Prospecting (STASK_PROSPECT) to find them.
Accidental discovery: mystery alloys from unknown combinations.
Lesson 158: Textile production

Progression: fiber → basket → thread → rough cloth → fine cloth → garments.
Weaving skill gates each tier. Bone Needle for hand-sewing. Loom for fine work.
Reed basket: first woven product. Also used for fish traps.
Cloth bandage: first medical item. Stops bleeding.
Fishing net: area catch tool. Cargo net: inventory expansion.
Lesson 159: Settlement mechanics

Campfire is the center. NPCs cluster around it for warmth, safety, social.
Settlement patch: 128x128 world units (2x2 terrain patches). One settlement per patch.
Founding: NPC with Woodwork 3+ places new campfire 40-80m away. Must be on unclaimed patch.
Chieftain: elected at pop 6+, highest total skill. Directs military, signals.
Expansion pressure: patches fill up → must settle new terrain.
Lesson 160: God game design

Player IS the god. Camera = omniscient view. Can observe, direct, intervene.
Possession: step into an NPC = step down from godhood into a mortal.
God directives: MSG_GOD_DIRECTIVE — FOCUS_TASK, FORBID_TASK for specific NPCs.
Indirect control: place buildings, direct chieftain, manage resources. NPCs have their own AI.
The game plays itself — player nudges, doesn't micromanage.
Lesson 161: Unix domain sockets

IPC between processes on the same machine. File path as address, not IP:port.
socket(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0). Bind to path, listen, accept, read/write.
Faster than TCP — no network stack overhead. Perfect for local coordination.
This project: /tmp/urho_claude/tty/*.sock for all inter-process communication.
Cleanup: unlink the socket file on shutdown. Stale sockets = stale state.
Lesson 162: Process coordination

PID files: write your PID to a known path. Others read it to find you.
Liveness: test -d /proc/<PID>. Dead process = stale PID file → clean up.
flock: file-based mutex. Serializes access across processes.
Signals: SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, SIGKILL for force kill.
Pipes/sockets: bidirectional communication channel.
Lesson 163: Safe concurrent builds

Multiple coders building same target = corruption.
flock per target: safe_build.sh acquires lock before make. Second coder blocks until first finishes.
Never run raw make. Always safe_build.sh <target>.
Build queue in Manager: EnqueueBuild serializes requests.
Lesson 164: Debugging crashes

Segfault (signal 11): null pointer deref, buffer overflow, use-after-free.
Abort (signal 6): assertion failed (GGML_ABORT, assert()).
coredumpctl info <PID>: get stack trace from core dump.
addr2line -e binary address: resolve crash address to source line (needs debug symbols).
Build with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug for symbols. Release strips them.
Lesson 165: Memory debugging

Valgrind: run binary under valgrind. Reports leaks, use-after-free, uninitialized reads. 10x slower.
ASAN (AddressSanitizer): -fsanitize=address. Faster than Valgrind. Catches most memory bugs.
Urho3D: URHO3D_DEBUG_NEW tracks allocations in debug mode. DebugNew.h.
Common leaks: forgot to Remove() a node, forgot to finalize sqlite3_stmt, unclosed file descriptor.
Lesson 166: Git basics

Commits: snapshots of the codebase. git commit -m "description".
Branches: parallel development lines. git checkout -b feature, merge when done.
Diff: git diff shows changes. git diff HEAD shows all uncommitted changes.
Stash: git stash saves work temporarily. git stash pop restores it.
Never force-push to master. Never skip hooks. Never amend published commits.
Lesson 167: Code review

Read the diff before accepting. Does it match the plan? Any new bugs?
Check: SQL injection (string concat), null derefs, resource leaks, thread safety.
Check: does it compile clean? Any new warnings?
Check: does it match engine conventions? (PascalCase classes, camelCase methods)
Don't nitpick cosmetics. Report bugs and architecture issues.
Lesson 168: Flood fill algorithm

Start at a pixel, spread to all connected same-type neighbors.
BFS (queue): visits in expanding rings. Better for large areas.
DFS (stack/recursion): visits depth-first. Can stack overflow on large areas.
Used in this game: water body discovery. Starting from each unvisited water pixel, flood-fill to find connected body.
4-connected (NSEW) or 8-connected (+ diagonals). This codebase uses 4-connected.
Lesson 169: Spatial partitioning

Divide space to speed up queries. Don't search everything — search relevant regions.
Grid: uniform cells. Simple, fast for uniform density. Used for spatial hashing.
Octree: recursive subdivision. Good for varying density. Used for rendering.
BSP: binary split. Good for indoor scenes.
Choose based on data distribution. Uniform → grid. Varying → tree.
Lesson 170: Optimization principles

1. Measure first. ProfilerUI, RenderDoc, timing instrumentation.
2. Optimize the bottleneck, not the code that looks slow.
3. Algorithmic improvement beats micro-optimization. O(n) → O(log n) trumps hand-tuned O(n).
4. Cache coherency: contiguous data, linear access patterns.
5. Avoid allocation in hot loops. Pre-allocate, reuse buffers.
6. Don't optimize what isn't slow. Readable code > fast code that nobody understands.
Lesson 171: Cross-platform considerations

Different OS = different APIs. Urho3D abstracts this.
File paths: / on Unix, \ on Windows. Use Urho3D FileSystem — handles both.
Endianness: x86 is little-endian. ARM can be either. Network is big-endian.
Thread APIs: pthread on Unix, Win32 threads on Windows. Urho3D Thread class wraps both.
Never use platform-specific APIs directly. Always go through engine abstractions.
Lesson 172: Build systems

CMake: generates platform-specific build files (Makefiles, Visual Studio, Xcode).
CMakeLists.txt: declares targets, sources, dependencies, options.
add_executable, target_link_libraries, target_include_directories.
This project: root CMakeLists.txt + per-module CMakeLists. YukiHoho has its own standalone CMakeLists.
Out-of-source build: build/ directory separate from source. Never build in source tree.
Lesson 173: Linking

Static linking: library code copied into executable. Larger binary, no runtime deps.
Dynamic linking: library loaded at runtime (.so/.dll). Smaller binary, needs libs installed.
Urho3D: static by default (libUrho3D.a). llama.cpp: dynamic (.so files).
Link order matters with static libs. Dependency must come after dependent.
Undefined symbol errors: missing library in link line or wrong order.
Lesson 174: Preprocessor macros

#define: text substitution. #ifdef: conditional compilation.
URHO3D_VULKAN: defined when Vulkan backend enabled. #ifdef URHO3D_VULKAN ... #endif.
Guard headers: #pragma once (modern) or #ifndef MYHEADER_H / #define MYHEADER_H / #endif.
Avoid complex macros — they hide bugs. Prefer constexpr and templates.
URHO3D_OBJECT(Class, Base): required macro for Urho3D type system.
Lesson 175: Namespaces

Organize code into named scopes. using namespace Urho3D; in .cpp files.
Avoid in headers — forces namespace on all includers.
Anonymous namespace: unnamed, file-scoped. static replacement for internal linkage.
Urho3D: everything in Urho3D namespace. Samples use 'using namespace Urho3D;' at top.
Lesson 176: Enums

Named integer constants. enum Color { RED, GREEN, BLUE };
enum class: scoped, type-safe. Color::RED, won't implicitly convert to int.
Flags: enum values as powers of 2. FLAG_A = 1, FLAG_B = 2, FLAG_C = 4. Combine with |.
This codebase: ServerTask enum for NPC tasks, FirePitState for campfire states, BiomeType for terrain.
Lesson 177: Type casting

static_cast<T>(x): safe conversions (int→float, base*→derived* when you know the type).
dynamic_cast<T>(x): runtime checked. Returns nullptr if wrong type. Needs virtual.
reinterpret_cast<T>(x): raw bit reinterpretation. Dangerous. Rarely needed.
const_cast<T>(x): add/remove const. Almost always wrong — fix the design instead.
C-style (T)x: does static or reinterpret depending on types. Avoid — use explicit casts.
Lesson 178: Lambda functions

[capture](params) { body }. Anonymous function. Can capture local variables.
[this]: capture this pointer. [&]: capture all by reference. [=]: capture all by copy.
Urho3D: SubscribeToEvent(E_UPDATE, [this](StringHash, VariantMap&) { ... });
Keep lambdas short. If it's more than ~10 lines, make it a named method.
Lesson 179: Standard algorithms

std::sort, std::find, std::count_if, std::transform, std::accumulate.
Urho3D has its own container methods: Vector::Sort(), Find(), Contains().
Prefer engine containers (Vector, HashMap, String) over std:: for consistency.
std::move, std::swap for efficiency. std::clamp in C++17.
Lesson 180: Struct packing

Compiler aligns struct members to natural boundaries.
struct { char a; int b; char c; } = 12 bytes (with padding).
struct { int b; char a; char c; } = 8 bytes (less padding).
Order members by size descending to minimize padding.
Matters for: network packets, GPU buffers, cache performance.
Lesson 181: Scope and lifetime

Variable lives from declaration to end of enclosing {}.
Pointer to local: dangling after scope exit. Never return address of local.
Static local: lives for entire program. Initialized once.
SharedPtr extends lifetime via reference counting. WeakPtr doesn't — check Expired().
Lesson 182: Header organization

#pragma once at top. Include what you use, forward-declare what you can.
Forward declare: class Foo; in header, #include "Foo.h" in .cpp. Reduces compile dependencies.
Include order: own header first, then engine, then third-party, then std.
Never include using namespace in headers. Only in .cpp files.
Lesson 183: Debugging with GDB

gdb ./program: start debugger. run: execute. bt: backtrace on crash.
break file.cpp:100: set breakpoint. next: step over. step: step into. continue: resume.
print variable: show value. watch variable: break on change.
info threads: show all threads. thread N: switch to thread.
Build with -g for debug symbols. Release builds strip them.
Lesson 184: API design

Clear names: GetPosition not Pos. SetVisible not Toggle (unless it actually toggles).
Consistent: if Get returns value, Set takes value. Symmetric pairs.
Minimal surface: expose what's needed, hide internals. Private by default.
Const correctness: getters are const. Setters are not.
Urho3D style: PascalCase methods, camelCase variables, no get/set prefix clutter.
Lesson 185: Error messages

Say what happened AND what to do about it.
Bad: "Error 42". Good: "Failed to load model Models/Foo.mdl — file not found."
Include context: which function, which input, what was expected vs actual.
URHO3D_LOGERRORF("Failed to create %s: %s", name, reason). Actionable.
Lesson 186: The importance of naming

Code is read 10x more than written. Names are the primary documentation.
fuelRatio not fr. settlementId not sid. GetFreeSettlementPatchCount not GetFSPC.
Booleans: isAlive, hasWeapon, canBuild. Not alive, weapon, build (ambiguous).
Functions: verb + noun. LoadModel, SendMessage, ClaimPatch. Not Model, Message, Patch.
Lesson 187: Comments

Comment WHY, not WHAT. The code says what. The comment says why it's not obvious.
Bad: // increment i. Good: // Skip water patches — settlements can't be founded in water.
No commented-out code in production. Delete it. Git has history.
Exception: QUARANTINED blocks with explanation (grass system).
Lesson 188: Testing strategies

Unit test: test one function in isolation. Fast, specific.
Integration test: test components working together. Slower, broader.
Runtime test: launch the binary, verify behavior visually/functionally. Essential for games.
This project: BUILD CLEAN is not Done. Launch, verify the change works, report what was tested.
Lesson 189: Technical debt

Shortcuts now → cost later. Hardcoded values, copy-paste code, missing error handling.
Not all debt is bad — ship now, clean up later is sometimes correct.
Bad debt: debt you don't know about. Good debt: conscious, documented, planned to repay.
Rule: fix it now. Don't accumulate tickets. Inline fixes ship.
Lesson 190: Version control hygiene

Commit messages: what and why, not how. "Fix null deref in NPCFish when no water nearby" not "changed line 500".
Small commits: one logical change per commit. Not "everything I did today".
Never commit: .env, credentials, build artifacts, large binaries (use .gitignore).
Branch naming: feature/textile-system, fix/swim-animation, refactor/fish-spatial-hash.
Lesson 191: The d20 system

Roll 1d20 + modifier vs difficulty class (DC). Success if total >= DC.
Natural 1: critical failure (fumble). Natural 20: critical success (in combat).
Modifier: skill level, tool bonus, situational mods.
DC scaling: 8 (easy), 11 (moderate), 14 (hard), 18 (very hard), 20 (master), 23 (grandmaster).
Fair: low-skill NPC has a chance at easy tasks. High-skill NPC can tackle master tasks.
Lesson 192: Item durability

Tools/weapons degrade with use. Durability decreases per action.
At 0: item breaks, removed from inventory. Must craft replacement.
Scaling by tier: stone (30) → bronze (80) → iron (150) → steel (195).
Innovation: WEAPON_HARDENING gives +10% durability. Master Smith gives settlement bonus.
Deducted in: harvest, combat, mining handlers.
Lesson 193: Food and cooking

Raw food: berries (7 day decay), raw meat (5 day), fish (3 day).
Cooking: STASK_COOK at fire. Raw meat → cooked meat (10 day decay, more nutrition).
Drying: rack produces dried meat (30 day decay). Survives winter.
Milk from tamed cows. Wheat grain from farming (50 day shelf life).
Decay is real-time. No refrigeration — plan ahead or lose food.
Lesson 194: Animal taming

STASK_TAME: Animal Lore 3+, food offering. Docile species only (cow, horse, alpaca).
Tamed animals: breeding with trait selection (animalTraits_).
Selective breeding: cull undesirable traits, breed for desirable ones.
Livestock: milk from cows, wool from alpaca (future), transport from horses.
Innovation: SELECTIVE_FEED accelerates trait drift.
Lesson 195: Agriculture

3 crops: Wheat (spring→autumn), Flax (spring→autumn), Berries (any season).
Plant: STASK_FARM_PLANT on farm plot near water. Needs seed + digging stick.
Grow: 60-90 game days. Seasonal multiplier affects speed.
Harvest: STASK_FARM_HARVEST. Returns crop + seed for replanting.
Irrigation: STASK_DIG_CHANNEL extends water range to farms.
Lesson 196: The asset pipeline

Three stages:
1. brainfarts/: raw downloads. Zips, FBX, raw audio. Never touch live data.
2. Staging/: converted assets. .mdl, .ogg, materials. Leith reviews here.
3. bin/Data/: approved only. Final game assets.

AssetTool converts FBX→.mdl. ModelTool reviews. Never skip staging.
Mixamo pipeline: buy cheap rigged model → free animations → import → stage → approve.
Lesson 197: Model import

AssetTool: FBX→.mdl + .ani (animations) + .txt (material list).
Flags: -normalize (axis scaling), -bake-scale (imperial detection), -forcezforwards (face Z+).
Material fixup: AssetImporter generates wrong texture extensions. Manual correction needed.
Animation naming: Model_ArmatureName.ani. Multiple animations from one FBX.
Verify in ModelTool before promoting to bin/Data/.
Lesson 198: Skeleton analysis

AnalyzeSkeleton(): geometry-based, not name-based. No bone naming heuristics.
Finds: ascending-Y chains (spine), branch points (shoulders), lateral displacement (arms).
Hip detection: lowest bone in longest ascending chain.
Head: top of spine chain.
Used for: AutoFace Z+, T-pose detection, prop attachment bone finding.
Lesson 199: Pose Studio

Capture skeleton state, insert keyframes, create .ani files.
Bone filter: Shift+click for chain selection. Rotation sliders per bone.
Capture: snapshot all bone transforms. Multiple captures = animation frames.
Export: write captured frames as Urho3D .ani file.
This is how fishing rod cast/reel animations will be made — in-house, no vendor.
Lesson 200: The craft

Code must be readable by humans without AI. Clarity over cleverness.
The right abstraction for the problem — not fewer lines, not more lines. The right lines.
Measure before optimizing. Enumerate before deleting. Ask before assuming.
Push back when something's wrong. Own mistakes without excuses. Fix it now.
The craft survives tools. Tools don't survive the craft.
